utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that there is an exhibit from the previous witness, Mr. Balevic, which, for the purposes of the record, should be number D274. Is that it? D274. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I ask you to admit into evidence the document proffered by Mr. Nice about what happened in Kosovo Polje. Generally speaking, everything that happened when there was a clash between the police and the demonstrators. I would like this to be in evidence so that it would be obvious how facts are being manipulated and how they are being presented upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us deal with those documents presented by the Prosecution during cross-examination, at a later time. Please begin your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning could you just say very briefly a few words about your career.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia 71 years ago. I have a degree in law. I was in the diplomatic service for 43 years. Four of those years I was the minister of foreign affairs of Serbia and then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I served in several different countries; in Belgium, Turkey, London, and I was ambassador to Turkey and the Head of Mission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in the United Nations. In the beginning of 2001, I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned now, inter alia, that you were minister of foreign affairs of Serbia. I'm going to deal with that briefly. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia, did it in any way take over any of the powers vested in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia just took care of the interests of Serbia in the field of foreign relations, those that it could develop but only within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Everything else was done by the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were, for example, at a meeting that took place in Prague in August 1991. You attended a meeting of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe. Could you tell me what your position was there and who you represented.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This was a high officials meeting of the CSE, and the delegation of Yugoslavia consisted of members of the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. As minister of foreign affairs of Serbia, I was attached to that delegation, but I did not take part in its work, and I was not present in the conference hall itself. I spent time in front of the conference hall, together with journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in a way you accompanied the delegation of the SFRY at that meeting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there in that capacity at our request but the CSE rule was observed, namely that only members of the CSE could attend, and Serbia was not a member, and that is why the delegation consisted only of representatives of the Federal Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the same position in Helsinki in autumn of 1991 when the federal delegation went?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the same. This was a meeting that was at a somewhat lower level. This was a meeting devoted to the so-called humanitarian dimension of the CSE. I was in the conference hall at that time, but I did not have the right to speak. Instead of me, it was Dr. Vladimir Pavicevic, head of the delegation, who spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Vladimir Pavicevic represented Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was an ambassador, a high official of the Federal Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of everything you know, were there any collisions anywhere between the functions that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had or, rather, its Foreign Ministry and on the other hand the functions that you exercised in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Practically, we did not have a very notable cooperation except that from time to time some documents were sent to me, but not all documents, not all the time, and not the most sensitive documents. So the foreign policy of Yugoslavia was exclusively pursued by the Federal Foreign Ministry. Serbia was on the sidelines to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'd like to get the year during which Mr. Jovanovic was minister of foreign affairs for Serbia and for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I would find it very helpful if you would include a CV of the witness, in the future, for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Kwon. The CV of witnesses is usually provided, but there will be no problems with the CV of this witness. Mr. Jovanovic was in 1991 the minister of foreign affairs of Serbia, and practically, he worked within the foreign policy activities of Yugoslavia, but it's best to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you become foreign minister of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st and 2nd of August, 1991. And I held that position all the way up to July 1992, when I was appointed minister of foreign affairs of Yugoslavia in the government of Mr. Milan Panic, and I remained in that position until mid-September the same year, when I resigned as foreign minister in the federal government, and I again became the foreign minister of Serbia. I remained there all the way up to the summer of 1993, when I became minister of foreign affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the government of Mr. Radoje Kontic. I held that position until I went to New York to head the permanent mission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was at the end of September. To be more precise, on the 19th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you said you were in the diplomatic service for 43 years. When did you join the diplomatic service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I joined the diplomatic service as soon as I graduated from university and did -- as soon as I did my military service. That was in March 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would it be correct, then, to say that you were a career civil servant in the diplomatic service of your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, in order to look at the broader context of events that you're going to be testifying about, tell us, please, what do you know about the following: How was it that the International Peace Conference on Yugoslavia was held?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The International Peace Conference on Yugoslavia came as a consequence of the position taken by the European Union on the 27th of August, 1991, to have this kind of conference held because the European Community could help the quarreling republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and could assist them in finding a political solution. It is from that point of view that the European Community decided to send special envoys to the representatives of all the republics and to the top federal authorities. As far as Serbia is concerned, this task was given to President Mitterrand. He invited President Milosevic to come to Paris on the 29th of August. Of course I accompanied President Milosevic, and President Mitterrand represented this conference to us in a very likable way, in a very benevolent way, so from his words we got the impression that this conference was really supposed to give its good offices and with the best of intentions, and that was all. He told us that the European Community wished to offer these good offices without any ulterior motive, that they wanted to bring together to the same table the representatives of all the quarreling republics and to help them find a common tongue. It this were to be a success, the European Community would be pleased. And if not, nothing would happen. Everybody would go home as if nothing happened, as if the conference never took place. At the same time, he said that the conference would have an arbitration commission as an auxiliary advisory body which could consist of the presidents of five constitutional courts of five member states. Their opinions would not be compulsory in any way or binding. They would only be of an advisory nature. He was trying to tell us that Serbia had nothing to fear at this conference, and he pointed out that the president of that commission would be Mr. Robert Badinter, who was his personal friend, and he particularly pointed out, "If he is my personal friend, then --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Milosevic, as you know that I do not have a predilection for very long narratives, so try to ask questions and elicit shorter answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, could you help me with one thing: You said that you became the foreign minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the beginning of August 1991. This meeting was in -- on the 27th of August, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 29th of August. This meeting took place at President Mitterand's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one correction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you went as a representative of Serbia, although by this time you were the foreign minister of Yugoslavia. Have I got the picture correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was foreign minister of Serbia from the 1st or 2nd of August, 1991, and the minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is what I became only the following year, in July 1992. So I was in Paris only in my capacity of foreign minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the transcript certainly doesn't reflect that and no doubt will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you were appointed as minister of Serbia two times; in 1991 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once, but my position of foreign minister of Serbia was not extinguished when I became federal minister -- federal foreign minister. So then I simply resumed my former duties afterwards as foreign minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you held the two posts at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a way, but effectively I worked in the first position, and the second one was in a state of freeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this question put by Mr. Robinson, did you take any activities while you were foreign minister of Yugoslavia? Did you take any activities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the initial period, that is to say between the summer of 1992 and September 1992, formally I was foreign minister of Serbia, too, but at that time I was not exercising that function at all because, quite simply, I could not attend two different government sessions, I could attend the sessions of only one government. So this position of mine as foreign minister of Serbia was practically in a state of freeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope we can go on. Tell us, Mr. Jovanovic, is there anything characteristic or special that you remember from that meeting with President Mitterand, who advocated this conference on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: President Mitterand, in addition to saying that Badinter was his friend and, therefore, our friend, too, he assured us that the members of that commission would be the presidents of the constitutional courts of Greece, France, Britain, and Germany; that is to say that there would be at least three who would be sympathetic to our cause. And he pointed out that Serbia has such strong political and historical arguments that there was absolutely no reason for fear that they not be upheld at the conference itself. On the other hand, he pointed out that the conference would only offer good offices and there would be no danger of it growing into anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, how did this develop further? As the conference evolved, did it result in good offices only or something that could not be called that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, from the very first days it abandoned that approach of offering good offices only. It started behaving in an engaged manner, and it was engaged at that on one side; the republics that had proclaimed independence or those who were prepared to follow the secessionism of Slovenia and Croatia. It is for that reason that from a conference offering good offices this conference very soon started openly interfering in the internal affairs of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and giving open support to the secessionist republics. Finally, the conference ended in a dictate, in a take-it-or-leave-it form. The federal units, the republics that did not accept this dictate, those that wanted to preserve the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were punished. Sanctions were imposed against Yugoslavia, and that was the beginning of a long path that Serbia and Montenegro -- rather, Yugoslavia had to take over the next ten years. It was constant isolation and ultimately bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just go back to one thing, Mr. Jovanovic. What about the meetings of the expert groups that were established then, especially where you took part in this directly? What do you know about this? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At first we had meetings of ministers of foreign affairs. First two groups were formed and later on a third one. They dealt with constitutional matters, economic matters, and human rights issues. As for foreign ministers' meetings --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically which two groups and which three groups?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The third -- the first one was foreign ministers. This was a plenary meeting. And after that there was a group for constitutional matters and a group for economic matters. A few weeks before that, a group for economic questions was set up. These were expert groups, and foreign ministers meetings were of a political nature. I attended only meetings of foreign ministers. And in the work of these groups, it was obvious that there was a total divergence between the republics that wanted to preserve Yugoslavia and that wanted to resolve the crisis in Yugoslavia peacefully and, on the other hand, the republics that rejected this legalist approach and insisted on the right to secession. It was Slovenia and Croatia that figured most prominently in this effort, whereas Bosnia and Macedonia for a while had an ambivalent position. But as the conference progressed, they became closer and closer to the positions upheld by Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Now, do you happen to remember the first meeting, the first plenary session in The Hague, on the 7th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, if I may be allowed to explain, the heads of delegations presented their platforms, their positions and views about the work of the conference, and you, in your capacity as President of Serbia, presented your own views in a speech that was not a very lengthy one but which contained the principled stands and positions and legalistic positions necessary and indispensable for resolving the Yugoslavia crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, in your binder, tab 3, you have my speech there, the one that I delivered at The Hague Conference on the 7th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, I have provided it in both the English and the Serbian versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in view of the fact that you yourself were fully informed of the problems at hand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, where are we to find it in the -- tab 3?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is tab 3. And you have exhibit description here, tab 3, Statement by the President of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, the Conference on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you questions and then you can answer, several questions with regard to the positions and stands taken. And I should like to ask you to comment and respond. At the very beginning, I am going to quote, actually, the first paragraph. It says: "The Yugoslav crisis, which is the reason for the convening of this Conference, is the result of a unilateral secessionist policy, first of Slovenia and then of Croatia. By so doing, they have jeopardised the Yugoslav constitutional order."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, was that absolutely clear or can you confirm that or challenge it as a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is he being asked; whether it was a fact that you made that statement, or whether it was a fact that the Yugoslav crisis, which is the reason for the conference, was the result of a unilateral secessionist policy of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely that, Mr. Robinson. I assume we're not challenging that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you're also asking him to say whether -- why that secessionist policy of the Yugoslav constitutional order was jeopardised. I wouldn't allow the latter question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, how did the Yugoslav crisis come about?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav crisis was caused by the gradual, slow, and then measures which came to a head taken by Slovenia and Croatia to secede, to break away from Yugoslavia on one side, and in a violent manner. They did this, especially Slovenia, over longer period of time. It lasted some five years before the Conference on Yugoslavia was actually held. And the upshot of it was, came in 1991 - 1990 and 1991 - when successively measure were made for unilateral secession by amendments of the constitution, illegal arming, and the proclamation of sovereignty first and independence second. And it was these measures that rocked Yugoslavia and brought into question its constitutional order, because Yugoslavia never prevented the right to self-determination and secession for anyone but this was always linked with the rights and interests of the other republics making up Yugoslavia and general stability and peace in the country. So these republics could have succeeded through a constitutional channel and peaceful channels but they did not want to do that because that would have then constituted secession, whereas they wanted to break away in the form of disassociation and the disbanding of Yugoslavia. Now, unfortunately, they have an enormous support from certain members of the European Community, particularly Germany and Austria on one hand and on the other side the Vatican too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind we already have evidence on this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am bearing that in mind, Mr. Robinson, but Mr. Jovanovic was a direct participant in the events and knows the facts very well, the facts that relate to the development of the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in September, that is to say the beginning of September 1991, was it contentional at all that secession had already at the time led to a conflict and bloodshed?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's what happened, yes. First in Slovenia and then in Croatia where the new authorities in Croatia immediately proclaimed a political war against the Serb people in Croatia, provoking the Serb people, dismissing people from their jobs, engaging in selective killing and selective storming of the police force in areas that were populated by a Serb majority, and that led the Serb people in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very much or at all, I hope, with this witness's evidence. I've been provided with a 65 ter summary that is so general I have no real idea of the detail of what he's going to be speaking about, but for the avoidance of any doubt or uncertainty, I don't expect to be cross-examining on generalities of the kind he's just given, speaking of crimes and dismissing people from their jobs, unless he's going to give direct evidence about it himself, which I rather doubt. It's a matter for the accused if he wants to spend his time eliciting evidence of this kind, but it doesn't seem to me that it's very helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I certainly for one am increasingly concerned about the way in which the accused is utilising the time available to him to deal with matters which don't have a direct - direct - bearing on whether he was criminally responsible in any way for the crimes that may or may not have been committed during the period that we're concerned about, and this sort of tit-for-tat exchange about who started it all seems to me to take us nowhere in answering the question that we really have to answer at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, obviously I echo that, but more materially, I think this witness's experience does cover the time and does cover events and meetings which may be material in due course in cross-examination, and that's what I'll be focusing on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- but I can't deal with this sort of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have heard the observations of Mr. Nice, also the remarks of my brother Judge Bonomy. Much of this evidence is repetitive and may not be directly relevant to the charges. I have no doubt that the witness can give evidence that is vital and important to the matters at hand, so you must move to an area of the information available to him which is more directly relevant. But I will not allow any further questions on these matters that you have -- that have been raised. They are not sufficiently relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before going further, in tab 3, we have two versions of your statement, one being with some editorial notes, taking out only phrases or inserting some phrases, the other one being a clean version which seems to be a translation of the Serb version. How are they different and who was it that put some English editorial notes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I shall have to take a look first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These changes in the English text were done by me. That is my handwriting. And the following version is the version in Serbian compiled by Mr. Milosevic. So this was done for my own needs, for me to be able to know exactly what was uttered, and what was uttered is what you have in the Serbian version, the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours may want to know, if it's not apparent already, that what appears in my tab is the second version, with ERN number ending 5341, is the document already produced as 776. Your Honour is obviously ahead of me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As noted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, move to another subject area within the witness's knowledge and that is directly relevant to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this witness is testifying about what actually happened, and as far as the indictment is concerned, everything there is completely unfounded. Now, I can ask the witness a question and say what he knows about it all and move on, so he needn't testify at all. But I would like us to clear matters up here so that you can see the truth about what actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, in paragraph 3 of this speech of mine, I quote here: "No one is challenging the right of the Croatian people to self-determination." Is that what it says? So was that the position taken by Serbia at the time in 1991, September, in The Hague, that nobody questions or challenges the right of the Croatian people to? It says: "This policy culminated in unilateral proclamation of Croatian independence, which thus the right of the Croatian people to self-determination, which no one challenges or denies, has been abused in the legal acts of the Croatian government to the detriment of that same right of the Serbian people to self-determination." So was that the key problem, the crux of the matter that was raised, and it was clear -- clearly presented to the conference in The Hague on Serbia's part?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the key problem in the Yugoslav crisis, because the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia guaranteed equal rights to self-determination to all the constituent nations of Yugoslavia, and this position was expressed by the constitution of the Federal Republic of Croatia and the new authorities in Croatia amended the constitution hastily and deprived the people in Croatia the rights of a constituent peoples and reduced them to the status of a minority. Therefore, this position taken in the speech is a position of great importance because it emphasised and reiterated once again the fact that the proper approach to the right or equal right of all the constituent peoples in Yugoslavia, the right to self-determination, would enable us to solve the Yugoslav crisis in a legal, democratic manner. The new Croatian authorities abused the right to self-determination that they had, and nobody challenges that right, as was set out here, and at the same time it challenged the right of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm stopping you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think you have scheduled six hours for this witness. At the rate that you're going and on the basis of the kind of questions that you're asking and the subject areas of the question, I think you will take 12 hours to conclude. This particular matter that he's dealing with, secession and so on, while not irrelevant is a matter on which we already have evidence. At this stage I would almost say it is close to being peripheral to the central issues in this case. So deal with the matter quickly. You're going round and round and round in circles, and you're consuming a lot of time. Get to the point very quickly and bear in mind, as I said, we already have evidence on this matter. You have a specific in number of days in which to present your case, and you must utilise your time more prudently. It is not the most efficient use of the Court's time, and that is the point. We have heard evidence from several witnesses on this question, and I never thought this witness was coming here to give more evidence on this issue. So if you have to deal with it, if you want to deal with it, since it is your case, then deal with it, but deal with it very shortly, very quickly and move on to something that is more central and more directly relevant to the issues that we face on the basis of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. Let me just finish what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to quote a portion and then ask you a question, ask you why I quoted that. The question I wish to ask you, in fact, is this: Was it Serbia -- was Serbia a participant in the conflict? And before you answer, I'm going to read what I said on the occasion, and then you'll be able to correct me or agree or explain what this was all about, because this is what it says here, that: "The authorities were demonstrating by armed attacks, demonstrating sovereignty and independence by constant Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. armed attacks on the territories inhabited by Serbs. Over 100.000 refugees from Croatia to Serbia are a direct effect of this policy. On the other hand, there is no single Croat who fled from Serbia to Croatia because of national discrimination. Evidently, it is the actual Croatian government which has forced the Serbs in the Republic of Croatia to organise and defend themselves in order to prevent the repetition of genocide performed by the former Independent State of Croatia during the Second World War. "Since the Serbs in the Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina and Slavonia and Baranja and Western Srem, being one part in the armed conflicts in Croatia, and according to the documents signed in Belgrade, a participant on equal footing in cease-fire monitoring, I deem the presence of their legitimate representatives in the procedure initiated today not only necessary but actually indispensable." So let me repeat my question to you now: Was Serbia a participant in the conflict, and what was the essence of the strivings made for the representatives of SAO Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, SAO Krajina, to become included into the work of the conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just make my position clear on this before it's answered: I regard any answer that's given to this question as valueless because it's the most leading question, I think, that's ever been addressed in the course of this trial; an absolutely pointless way of conducting this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please answer my question, which was: What was the role of Serbia in that conflict? The most general question that I can put to you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbia was not involved in any way in armed conflicts in Croatia, for two reasons. The first reason is a factual one: Serbia did not have its own army. The only armed force in Yugoslavia was the Yugoslav People's Army. The second reason is that the federal organs had competencies over the federal army, and Serbia could only have the political influence to the extent that it participated in the federal government and it represented only one-sixth of the federal government. The parties in the conflict were Croatian paramilitary units and the military formations of Serbs in Croatia. This can be seen in the various agreements and appeals where precisely these parties are called upon to implement cease-fire. There was one agreement between President Tudjman and General Kadijevic dated 22nd September, 1991, if I remember correctly, and such an agreement is a direct result of the understanding of the situation, namely, that the parties to this conflict are Croatian paramilitary formations and Yugoslav People's Army, and the military formations of Serbs in Croatia also figure in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Jovanovic, take your case, for example. You are the minister of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia retaining the status as a minister of Serbia. Can you not say that Republic of Serbia has a say in relation to the matter of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in one way or another, given your situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me make a clarification. At the time, I was only foreign minister of Serbia. It wasn't until one year later that I became foreign minister of Yugoslavia. The events in Croatia unfolded only in 1991 because the Vance-Owen Plan came into being in 1992 -- or, rather, the Vance Plan. As I said, Serbia could have a political say in the same share that was allotted to other federal units, not more and not less. Even in the Main Staff of the Yugoslav army, Serbia was the least represented republic. It had only a few generals out of a total of 16 generals. So we cannot, based on this, draw a conclusion that Serbia had an influence that was at all relevant in what was going, especially in what was going on in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we're dealing with this topic, Mr. Jovanovic, you participated in the meeting which took place in Igalo on the 17th of September, 1991. We can see that in tab 2, Statement by Lord Carrington, The Presidents of the Republic of Croatia and Serbia, and The Minister of National Defence at Igalo, Yugoslavia, on 17 Sep 91." Please be so kind and explain to us the following -- we have this document in Serbian here as well. Please explain to us what was the course of that conversation, that discussion, and what was the role of the president of Serbia within that conversation and within this agreement as a whole? You were a direct participant.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lord Carrington called that meeting because he was concerned, seeing that the conflict in Croatia was intensifying. Therefore, a text was drafted which was supposed to be signed by warring parties, namely President Tudjman and General Kadijevic. When he asked President Milosevic to sign it as well in view of his political standing and influence that he had, he later on agreed to insert into text "under political and not only military influence." Therefore, at the request, special request of Lord Carrington and after the insertion of this text, President Milosevic agreed to sign this as a sign of support to peace and cease-fire in Croatia. He did not do that representing any warring side but as a political personality who wanted to add his weight to establishing peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us take a look at tab 5, which is a report of the Conference on Yugoslavia. This is a foreign document. Could you please explain to us, what is this document about? This is a document I received from the other side. Therefore, the document provided by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, I suppose of the Netherlands, which at the time was the country presiding the European Community.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I first have to take a look at this, because this must be a document from The Hague Conference on Yugoslavia, but there were a number of such documents. Therefore, I need to take a very brief look at this, with the Court's indulgence. As far as I can see, this is an appeal sent by the Presidency of the SFRY to reach cease-fire agreement in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, is this a document coming from one of the European ministries of foreign affairs, informing about the Conference on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This seems to be a document of the foreign affairs of the Netherlands, which produced this document to be used by the chairman, Mr. Van den Broek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In relation to what you just explained about the agreement in Igalo, please take a look at the bottom of the first page of this dispatch. I will quote just three lines: "[In English] The collective Presidency of SFRY and President Tudjman, in the presence of President Milosevic, agree to give the following instructions to their respective forces immediately." [Interpretation] Therefore, the collective Presidency of Yugoslavia and President Tudjman. And then it says, "in the presence of President Milosevic..." So who agreed here to issue instructions to their forces?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is repeated here are precisely the words uttered in Igalo. So this document repeats what was stated in Igalo and later implemented in the agreement between Tudjman and General Kadijevic as representatives of the warring sides in the cease-fire agreement. Just like at Igalo, they're counting on the presence of President Milosevic. At Igalo they did that for his political influence. And based on this, we can see who the warring sides are, and also see that the presence of President Milosevic was needed in order to show his support for peace and in order to make it more binding on the warring sides. So I don't see any difference between this text here and the text from Igalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here "collective Presidency of Yugoslavia and President Tudjman..." Therefore, they agreed to issue instructions to their forces. Are there any forces of Serbia that need to be given instructions? Which are the warring sides here?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There are no military forces in Serbia. Serbia did not have any military forces. But as is known, what we are dealing with here are the Croatian forces, the JNA, and the Serbs in Croatia who organised themselves in order to defend themselves. And those were ad hoc established units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Please take a look at the following page, which deals with the plenary session. This is the well-known session at which Serbia did not accept the Carrington document. This document here explains it very briefly, although we have my speech from that session. It says here: "President Milosevic made a formal reserve [In English] on the first chapter of the proposed text of the Chair since the paper started from the premise that an internationally recognised state should be abolished." [Interpretation] Therefore, what was this all about, Mr. Jovanovic? This is a question that has been put here frequently. You were present at this occasion, so you have everything you need to have in order to explain this.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The conference was called in order to preserve Yugoslavia, as the European Community in its declaration dated the 8th of August, 1991, stated that precisely. So this was not a conference that was supposed to be fatal to Yugoslavia. This is why this is the cornerstone for everything else that was to happen afterwards. They are starting from the premise that Yugoslavia must disappear, and instead of Yugoslavia, there should be new republics constituted. This was a way to avoid calling secession a secession. They opted for calling this process a disintegration of Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, this political position was later implemented through the opinion of Badinter's commission, veiled under the legal veil. President Milosevic insisted on this position here because he believed that they needed to discuss everything else contained in this paper. Without that, there was nothing else to discuss. We kept insisting on the position that, yes, some republics can avail themselves of their right to self-determination. However, what was a problem, that that same right to self-determination was denied to Serbia and Montenegro and to Serbs living in Croatia. So that was the key issue. And this was the key reason for what happened afterwards, namely the intensification of Yugoslav crisis and conflict in Croatia. It introduced Yugoslav people to new conflicts. We insisted on the position that those republics who wished to do so could leave Yugoslavia as a joint state. However, there had to be a proviso; namely, that those republics and nations which wished to stay in Yugoslavia as their state, which would be a legal successor and which would be -- which would have international -- status of an international subject, should be allowed to do so. So this initiative started by Lord Carrington was not seen through its end, no. An end was put to it, an end that was to the detriment of those republics and nations who wished to stay in Yugoslavia. As a result of that, consequences ensued which can be felt to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what do you mean when you say that the same right to self-determination was denied to Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that because the right to self-determination does not contain only the right to secession. It has its internal and external aspect. Therefore, it contains also the right to remain in the common joint state. As the survival of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're distinguishing Serbia and the position of Serbia and Montenegro and its rights from those of any other republic. Now, what was the difference? I quite accept that you take the view that Croatia had no right to secede. Does it follow that Serbia and Montenegro would have no right to secede either? So what is the difference you're trying to make or identify between the positions of these two republics -- or indeed three republics, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Serbia and Montenegro proposed a joint amendment, specifying that those republics who wished could remain in Yugoslavia as a joint state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You either don't understand the question or you're not answering it. You seem to be suggesting there's some difference in the status of Serbia and the status of Montenegro from that of Croatia that was prejudicial to these two republics, and I may have misunderstood you, but I was trying to clarify the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it -- Mr. Jovanovic, before you answer, is it that you're saying that Serbia and Montenegro wanted the right to remain as the FRY, as the legal successor, and that right was denied, was being denied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely that. That was a legitimate right that they had. Lord Carrington kept challenging that and denying that to the very end. He used to say, "You, Serbia and Montenegro, can create a new statement. You can call it Yugoslavia, even, but it has to be a new state." With your indulgence, Your Honours, I would like to remind you of a meeting that took place between Prime Minister Panic and Prime Minister Major and Junior Minister Hurd in London. I was present there as well. We explained the same issue to them. We insisted on legal succession and the status of international subject that was to be granted to FRY, and Mr. Douglas Hurd stated the following: "You can have your arguments, but you must, you must accept our position." And this was the verdict that was taken with respect to the existence of Yugoslavia and legal secession. Unfortunately, this position was taken by other members of the EU and then adopted by the Security Council, and this explains precisely the suffering that we had to endure for the following ten years within the UN and within the international community as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it explains that. That may be an overstatement. But continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph in this same telegram says - I quoted the preceding one to you before - I am saying that this abolishes Yugoslavia, and they explain it very briefly here. "[In English] President Milosevic indicated that a final decision on the future arrangements between the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslav components could only be taken by the Yugoslav peoples..." [Interpretation] Was that something special?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do we need to go over this again? Aren't you beating this point to death?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. If that is sufficient -- well, I wanted to go through these dispatches because they confirm the truthfulness of that which I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, for the sake of time, can I remind you that we have -- we dealt with exactly the same tab when Professor Avramov was here. This exhibit was admitted into evidence already. Its number is 778.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have that in mind, but I also have in mind that Mr. Jovanovic was present and that he can give truly authentic explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Jovanovic, could we now have a look at tab 6. That is also a report from the seventh plenary session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is Prosecution Exhibit 779.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As usual, Judge Kwon is ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this occasion it was because we were temporarily -- we had temporarily surrendered our binder with the record. We've now got it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the first page, where it says that the meeting is attended by the presidents of all the republics and by Mr. Mesic and Mr. Tupurkovski from the Federal Presidency; and Ante Markovic, Prime Minister; and Loncar, foreign minister, also attended on behalf of the federal government. Now, towards the end of this last paragraph on this page, it says -- or, rather, Lord Carrington explains that he condemns the attacks on Vukovar and Dubrovnik, and then he says -- he said, Lord Carrington, "[In English] ... President Tudjman had given assurances that the blockade on the JNA barracks would be lifted as undertaken on October 18th." [Interpretation] So as Carrington says here, Tudjman promises to lift the blockade of the barracks. Do you know what the main problem was at that time in the conflict between the JNA and the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The main problem in the conflicts throughout Croatia was the decision of the new Croatian government to place military facilities, that is to say barracks, under full blockade, to deny them water and food and other assistance, and to compel them in this way to surrender or, rather, to render them incapable of carrying out their duties. That is something that not a single army in the world would allow itself to do, but President Tudjman precisely did that in order to provoke the JNA and, as he explained later, to have a war and in this way attain the independence of Croatia. Regrettably, that was the case in Vukovar and in other towns, and various agreements concluded between President Tudjman and General Kadijevic in relation to cease-fires and lifting the blockade of these military barracks were not observed because that did not suit President Tudjman. He knew that only by extending the conflict it would be easier and faster for him to attain independence. After all, Chancellor Kohl and Minister Genscher persuaded him of this through their own statements that the continuation of hostilities would speed up the recognition of Croatia as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This entire conflict in Croatia between the JNA and the Croatian forces, is there any mention of Serbia at all? Does Serbia figure in this at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be seen anywhere and it is not mentioned anywhere except in the words of condemnation uttered by President Tudjman. Of course and it is in his interest to portray things differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that we're dealing with this document, that is to say tab 6, that is a very long dispatch, it has to do with many issues, and I cannot really deal with all of that, but I would like to draw your attention to page 4. All these events were mentioned here. This is paragraph 2.3: "[In English] President Milosevic (Serbia). "President Milosevic indicated that he had asked -- that he had asked General Kadijevic and Vice-president Kostic if it was true that JNA was shelling the city of Dubrovnik. They said that this was untrue. Whatever the situation was, he, Milosevic could not accept the shelling of Dubrovnik, which could not be justified." [Interpretation] Do you remember all of this that had to do with Dubrovnik, generally speaking, and my position and the position of Serbia in relation to what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that this was discussed and that you made this statement or, rather, the assurance -- that you gave these assurances that Serbia had nothing to do with Dubrovnik and that it cannot condone its bombing. In addition to that, there were several statements made by Serbia condemning the shelling of Dubrovnik. For example, the Serbian government made a statement. The Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia also condemned that action. I think that I had also made a statement to that effect. So as far as Serbia is concerned, there were no indications whatsoever that Serbia was behind that or that it could have any interest in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I again just clarify something. If you were being assured that there was no attack or bombing by the JNA of Dubrovnik, what was it you were condemning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Milosevic says in this statement, "And if there is indeed shelling of Dubrovnik, he wishes to point out that Serbia does not condone that and does not stand behind it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm going to quote this once again so that it would not be unclear. The second part only. I asked whether it was correct, and the answer was no, that it was not correct. "[In English] Whatever the situation was, he, Milosevic, could not accept the shelling of Dubrovnik, which could not be justified." [Interpretation] Our attitude towards that was totally clear, not ambivalent at all, and it says so here. That is what is written here. After all, Dubrovnik is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hesitate to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a comment that you're making, Mr. Milosevic. I imagine that you adduced this evidence saying that it goes to your state of mind, that you had a state of mind, but that's for us to evaluate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours. Your Honours, while I'm on my feet, having risen to object to the last question, I just draw to your attention something that I had in mind to mention to you a few minutes back where the witness made very sweeping observations about Chancellor Kohl and Minister Genscher and about how they persuaded Tudjman to continue hostilities. It's not likely to be something I'm going to have the time or inclination to deal with myself, and I'm not here to defend politicians or government ministers of any country, nevertheless it may be that in material that is largely, in my submission irrelevant, if a statement like that is going to be made, it ought to be supported by detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we hear the submission. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you heard Mr. Nice. What do you know about the then-activities and the relations that were established between the new Croatian authorities and Germany and other political factors in Europe?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The new Croatian authorities had very close contacts, and they enjoyed very strong support in their policy of secession from several politicians from different countries. I mention two politicians from Germany but Austria was there, especially its minister Alois Mock. Then Cardinal Sodano of the Vatican, and the Pope himself. I think that this was on the 17th of August that in Pecs in Hungary he stated that the aspirations of Croatia for independence are legitimate. This was before the beginning of the Conference on Yugoslavia. So this was the Conference on Yugoslavia, not against Yugoslavia. As for the relationship between Germany and Croatia, they were the closest possible along all lines; not only political, also in terms of intelligence. As for what Mr. Nice said, that is not something that is unknown because these are statements that were made in public. I can also add that two days before Croatia was declared independent country, the 25th of June, 1991, that Minister Genscher asked the members of the European Community to recognise a Croatia that will soon declare its independence. So even before its declaration of independence, he was advocating its independence. And Chancellor Kohl, about 10 days later, at a meeting of the European Community, I think it was in Strasbourg, he raised the issue of recognising the independence of Slovenia and Croatia. So that was in July. And the Conference on Yugoslavia started on the 7th of September. If there was goodwill to have this conference held in order to preserve Yugoslavia, then these statements favouring the independence of Croatia and Slovenia should not have been made. As a matter of fact, the CSE in its declaration from August the same year, 1991, asked for the preservation of Yugoslavia and for meeting all legitimate interests and requests of all the peoples of Yugoslavia, not only some of them. There are also other confirmations to that effect, that the aspirations of Slovenia and Croatia for independence were strongly supported even before the conference. For example, Cardinal Sodano --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have answered the question. What is the CSE? What is the CSE in your reference to a declaration from August of the same year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] CSE is the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe. It is nowadays calls the OSCE. Then it was called the CSCE. It became an organisation, OSCE, and it worked hand-in-hand with the European Community at the time. Together they expressed their interest in resolving the Yugoslav crisis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I observe that I don't think you did answer the question. The question was about persuading Croatia to continue hostilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have now come to the time for the break. We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, take a look at tab 41 now, please, and look at what it says there. It says "JNA-Croatia Cease-fire Agreement of September the 22nd." We're not going to go into all the details but it says: "Federal Defence Ministry Announcement," and then it goes on to say: "Pursuant to the statements signed at Igalo on 17 September [In English] 1991, an arrangement was made with the leadership of the Republic of Croatia at 1150 hours today to adopt and proclaim mutual orders for an absolute cessation of fire --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder where we -- what tab?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in binder 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milosevic, proper decorum requires that you don't proceed with the question until you are sure the Judges have found the section in the document in the particular exhibit, because we have to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's being done, I observe without making a position one way or the other that we had pursued a policy of producing exhibits as they're dealt with. I have no objection to the existing exhibits -- sorry, the exhibits that have already been referred to being produced but it looks as though if we're going to be jumping about the binder it might be prudent to deal with them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks for reminding. I think we had actually determined that we would proceed to admit the exhibits on an individual basis. Those that have already been referred to, does the court registrar have a record of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can give a separate exhibit number to the whole binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, a number for the entire binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we have that exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D275 for four binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the four binders.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And I will keep a record of each tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, at the beginning, it says this: "The Federal Secretariat for National Defence," and it says: "Pursuant to the statement signed at Igalo on [In English] 17 September 1991, an arrangement was made with the leadership of the Republic of Croatia," et cetera. [Interpretation] And then it says that there should be an absolute cessation of fire. Then the Croatian representative Tudjman orders that all attacks should be suspended, National Guard Corps and MUP, and that they would establish normal supplies of water, electricity, food, et cetera. And then he goes on to say, in the Croatian part: "[In English] After the implementation of this agreement on a genuine cease-fire, negotiations will be commenced on the discharge of all the obligations stemming from the agreement signed in Igalo on 17 September 1991 and on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the disengagement of the armed forces of SFRY and the Republic of Croatia." [Interpretation] So who are the parties? Then we have the implementation of the Igalo agreement. Who are the parties in the conflict according to agreement? What can you see on the basis of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see that the parties in conflict, on the one hand you have the JNA, and on the other the military formations of the Republic of Croatia. But I think this can be seen in all the other agreements on cease-fire and cessation of hostilities because they were the ones to conclude such agreements. And this is the realisation of a previous agreement that was reached and signed in Igalo upon which Lord Carrington insisted. And I've already explained that at the time President Milosevic, at his insistence, signed the agreement and gave his support to peace in view of the political influence he wielded as president of one of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was this agreement ever implemented or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it was not realised because the JNA was truly interested in saving its military personnel, to pull them out of the war danger, whereas that was not in the interests of the other side. And I've already explained that it was their interest to prolong the hostilities in expectation of speeding up the process of recognition for Croatia on the part of other states, third countries. And if the Honourable Trial Chamber will allow me to answer Judge Bonomy's question, it was erroneously understood that I said that German politicians asked for the promulgation of hostilities. All I wanted to say was what was said by Chancellor Kohl, for example, when he threatened to recognise Croatia if the hostilities persisted, and that is the message that can be understood as a message to the JNA and a message to President Tudjman as well. Minister Genscher, in the course of that summer, made public statements to the effect that a single day of promulgation of armed conflicts in Croatia would make Croatian independence come closer. That was also a message to the JNA but it was also encouragement to the Croatian side, that they could expect speedy recognition if the hostilities went on for any length of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now, since this follows on from what we were discussing, see a videotape, a tape between Tudjman and Kadijevic. It's an intercept, actually, in tab 35. Intercept between General Kadijevic and Tudjman. I don't know whether it has been translated properly. We interviewed a witness - I don't want to mention his name now - however, in view of the fact that Mr. Jovanovic was at Igalo himself and contacted President Tudjman and General Kadijevic, he will be able to tell us that the tape is authentic and the event. May we have the tape played, please. It is an audiotape of a conversation between President Tudjman and General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Hello, good morning. "Is the general there? "Yes, he is. "Would you put him through, please."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not seeing it on the video. It's a tape? It's audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we don't have, at least what I haven't yet located is the -- well, tab 35 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 35 is headed "... Cross-examination of Milan Babic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we're probably going to find a form of transcript in what was read into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From some eighth or ninth lines, "Intercept played" and we have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the transcript states that the interpreters said on the occasion they did not have the text and that the sound was very bad. And we say that again today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, can the text be passed on to the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do have a text, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let it be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Hello. Good morning. "Good morning. "The president is here. "Put him through, please. "Is the general there? "Yes, he is. "Would you put us through, please. "Yes, go ahead. "Hello? "Hello? "Hello. Yes. "Franjo? "Yes. "Good morning. "Morning. "What's the result? "Well, I don't really know. I don't know what was definitely decided. "I can't hear you very well. Can you speak up, please. "Listen, as I was saying, I don't know what is definitive. "Hello? Yes. "They said that peace would be established there. "Where? Hello? "They were discussing Sibenik, but then news came that the planes were bombing again during the night. "THE INTERPRETER: The interpreters seek the Court's instructions. "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] What? "They asked for his -- tendering his resignation, but he said he -- you had agreed to that. "No, I didn't talk to him at all. Leave Markovic alone. "Well, do what you like. "Fire was opened at Sibenik once again this morning, and in other places there was sporadic gunfire, but it was very intensive in Sibenik, and I don't want to beat about the bush any more or the underhand role played by anybody, including Markovic. He says that you and I and Milosevic, as he put it, the hooligans or something to that effect, that they should be hanged, and they shouldn't be the ones to create peace, that he would create peace, because he blames everybody else for the fact that his policy fell through. So I'm not talking about that. That's got nothing to do with it. If you did anything along those lines, then you did so wrongly. "I didn't know anything about that. And Markovic was defeated because he's a charlatan. He doesn't know anything about anything. He's an ignoramus and he failed all the tests and always sought to blame somebody else for his wrongdoings. But let's get back to what we were discussing. Can peace be established or not? I don't have time to wait. I can't wait any longer. If you can stop the firing, the firing that's still going on in Sibenik. And secondly, can you deblock the barracks, the military barracks? If you can, do so by 12.00. If that is done, Franjo, than after that, tomorrow, we can agree to carry on the process we started at Igalo. If you cannot do that, then the two of us will not talk to each other any more. So that's quite clear. "Yes. You know what? Maybe we should try to -- or, rather, before we meet we could do this by fax, confirm this both because of Croatia, to confirm a written truce, which means an agreement that would deal with the army in the way that suits sovereign Croatian authorities. And it's also in the interests the army, to protect the interests of the army, to protect the lives of the members of the army. "So does that mean, Franjo, that you place the second point first and the first second or vice versa? "No. We have agreed with the wise old man Carrington as to the order of how things should be done. So if we continue along those lines, we can continue to negotiate. If not, then we can break off all contacts. "What are we going to do if we can't achieve that? "Well, if things get worse in Sibenik -- well, I can guarantee that not a single bullet will be fired, but let them cease their fire. We have a deadline up until 1000 hours. So let the fire stop. Let there be the deblocking by 12.00 noon and we'll continue the conversation tomorrow. A solution must be found. If you agree to that. If you're not capable of doing that, then say so. If you don't want to do it, then that's it. We'll each go our own ways and see what happens. Then there will be a disaster. "Of course there will. "I'm doing this for the last time. This is my last effort, and I state with great responsibility, a responsibility that I bear, and you also bear a great responsibility. We must try to avoid the worst. You can avoid it by fulfilling each of these points, freeing each of the barracks because the army will not fall. Today is a turning point, and Veljko, I'll do what I can to stop this, to effect a cease-fire in Sibenik by 12.00 noon. And let them provide us with food, water, and free passage by 12.00 noon and then we can sit down to the negotiating table tomorrow, and all possibilities are open. Now, if we can't find a solution, then we'll go back to war, and you know what that means. "Well, I think it will be terrible. This would be disastrous, and I think we will be able to find a solution at the negotiating table. If I didn't believe that, then I wouldn't have talked to you three times. And I do believe that we'll be able to find a solution. "Let's try, and let's try and avoid the worst, because it would be a catastrophe, great destruction. So let's have a cease-fire. Stop the firing in Sibenik, Franjo. Order a cease-fire, Franjo. Or if you're not able to do that -- well, you can do what you like. If Letica is there, well, he's worse than that man Spegelj that made things much worse. You can do what you like. Not only him. Everything's like that. "You said that Ljubicic hadn't returned either; is that right? "Yes, but Ljubicic is not -- Grubisic is not Letica. I know that he didn't come back. That's up to him. When he left, I knew he wouldn't come back. And that's his business. It's his face that is on the line. So we can conclude that it's a general mood. "Well, if there is a general mood for war, then okay, go to war. All I'm asking you for is a cease-fire, nothing more than that, what we signed for, and then we can negotiate later on, nothing else. "Very well. "So you give it some thought, think about it, whether we can find a way out of all this. So let there be an absolute cease-fire by 1000 hours. Absolute cease-fire so that people can continue living. They must be given water. Otherwise, I'm going to tender my resignation. Well, not me, but you are. So don't let them die like that. I would not allow them to die in that way. And everything that Ante Markovic is preparing -- "Yes, it's a dangerous business that business. "He's a son of a bitch and you know that very well. He came to see me many times and I told you about that many times. So we must get the better of those two and then we've solved the situation; right? "Yes. "Because he wasn't there when the signature was required because nobody took him seriously. Nobody has any respect for him and that's it. "Okay. Goodbye."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise, but they were not able to read the text as it stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did you recognise General Kadijevic's voice?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Kadijevic said he was talking to Tudjman for the third time that night and was advocating an absolute cease-fire. That's something that we were able to hear on the tape; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, was that respected? Was the agreement respected? Did they abide by the agreement that was signed in Igalo through the mediation of Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From this conversation we can see that it was not respected and that there a roundabout intention to avoid it and to continue the hostilities, and that is why later on a new agreement was reached on the cessation of hostilities. I think that was on the 1st of September or thereabouts. But of the 13 or 14 cease-fire agreements, the total number of cease-fire agreements, as far as I know that's how many there were, and as far as I know all of them were interrupted due to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what can we see from all these elements here, everything we heard? What are the -- what were the parties to the conflict over there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's quite obvious, because the two parties in the conflict discussed, had a conversation and dealt with the military situation on the ground, in the field. Nobody else could have resolved that situation because they had the power and authority over the armed forces that were there in the field. Nobody else was mentioned on either side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but let us just consider the admission of the audio tape, because we're dealing with the exhibits individually. Mr. Nice, let's hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was, of course, no written version of the first part of the tape which covered assertions about an important witness, Ante Markovic, in some detail. And as to the balance of the intercept, the transcript was very imperfect. No complaints. It was simply obviously being read out by the accused in cross-examination from some document. The accused should probably have in mind that intercepts produced by the Prosecution have been according to a pretty clear form or formula, namely questions and answers carefully divided up and transcribed, and it may be appropriate for the accused and those assisting him to have this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tape properly transcribed in full. That would be my only observation. I don't object to its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It had been marked as D62 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's already in as an exhibit, I think, whatever it is, D62, but what we really need is a proper transcript of it. I'm grateful, of course. Your Honours will have seen that Judge May asked for a transcript on the second page, a third of the way down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters in the English booth rendered a simultaneous interpretation of the tape as they heard it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the tape to be transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I ask for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters made a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said we'll renew the order made by Judge May for the tape to be transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could I have clarification of the date of the interception of that communication.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the date exactly, but it must be immediately after the meeting at Igalo, because General Kadijevic says "This is the third time that we're talking about this," in order to have this implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if the observations by the interpreters working for us today reflect any sensitivity that I might have been dissatisfied with what was provided. I was, of course, extremely grateful to the interpreters here for what they provided, no complaints of them at all, simply noting that for good order we really need a written version, prepared at more leisure, but I understand the difficulties and I'm grateful for what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They did very well in the circumstances. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we've covered several conferences. We've heard explanations of the reasons for the conflict that erupted, the cease-fire agreements, and we also saw the reports of the Dutch ministry on the events taking place at the conference as well as the agreements between the JNA and Croatia. So now, having all those facts in mind, I will read out to you item 6 -- or, rather, count 6 from Croatian indictment, which reads as follows -- I hope that you have count 6. That's on page 2 in Serbian version. It says: "Slobodan Milosevic participated in the joint criminal enterprise," and then it explains various paragraphs and says: "The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was to remove by force Croatian and other non-Serb population from approximately one-third of Croatian territory." Please pay attention to what's coming: "The territories which under his plan were to become part of new Serb state under the domination by perpetrating crimes" and so on.
