Mr. Jovanovic, these events, this series of events, including cease-fire agreements and events reflecting the situation in Yugoslavia at the time, does all of that confirm or deny this claim, or to be more precise, what plan, either plan created by myself or by Serbia, does it deal with? Was there a plan to remove the Croat and other non-Serb population from the approximately one-third of Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of such plan ever, and I don't think that such plan existed. Based on the facts that we heard, I don't think that one can conclude that there was such a joint criminal enterprise to achieve those goals. Moreover, it could be said that President Tudjman wanted not only to achieve independence by means of war but also wanted to get rid of the extra population, meaning Serbs, in Croatia by means of war. After the victorious operation called Storm in which several thousands of Serbs perished and which represented the greatest ethnic cleansing --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Objection. It's quite interesting to observe that the answer now being given is to a question that wasn't asked. It came out with remarkable facility, but it was not asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't asked, but it is still evidence. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can Mr. Jovanovic continue or need I put some additional questions to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and short answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, based on all the events that we covered very superficially in your testimony so far, who was involved in the conflict? Who was the victim? Who fought? Who perished? What was the origin of refugees and so on? Therefore, I put this question to you and read out this count of indictment, and based on that, please tell me, was there any plan on the Serb part to expel Croat and non-Serb population or did something else happen there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All facts point to something quite contrary, not what is stated in the indictment. Back in The Hague in September, at the time you stated that until that time, several thousands of Serbs fled from Croatia to Serbia, not only in the towns but also in other parts of Croatian territory where their lives were threatened. The conduct of Croat authorities had a very clear goal, namely to intimidate Serbs and to encourage them to flee. This mass expulsion, this mass exodus of Serbs culminated in the Operation Storm. President Tudjman, shortly after that, said in a gathering that Serbs will not constitute more than 3 to 5 per cent of Croatian territory ever in the future, which shows that this was an additional goal of Croatia in addition to achieving independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you just stated, is it related to the speech of Franjo Tudjman at a rally in Zagreb where he stated there would be no war had Croatia not wanted one? We've already seen this speech of his on a tape here. Do you remember him uttering those words, "There would be no war had Croatia not wanted one but we decided that was the way to achieve our goals"? Can you tell us what goals he referred to?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. And it is a bit unusual that President Tudjman so openly admitted that he favoured the war option in order to achieve his goals. What I tried to do was to show that he had several parallel goals. Independence was one goal, and then the other goal was to get rid of a large number of Serbs. And the events showed us in precisely what way he worked on achieving this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, all right, let us go back to the Conference on Yugoslavia. In tab 25, we have a letter by the vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia sent to the chairman of the Conference on Yugoslavia, Lord Carrington. This is a long letter which mentions that the Presidency of Yugoslavia on its session held on the December -- on 8th of December, 1991, examined the opinion of the Arbitration Commission sent by the conference secretary to the members of the Presidency and that it reached certain positions. Would you please elaborate on those positions.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this letter represented a challenge to this thesis from the second document of Lord Carrington to the effect that Yugoslavia ceased to exist and that it was in the process of disintegration and that therefore federal units had to be taken care of by placing them under a roof of newly independent states. And this letter states the facts showing that Yugoslavia still exists because more than half of its population continues to live in that country and that it is only the peoples of Yugoslavia who by way of referendum can decide whether their joint state can continue to exist. This was not an issue to be decided by any international forum. Furthermore, it states that Serbia and Montenegro, as well as Serbs living in other republics, remain loyal to their country, to their state which would continue to exist and that they do not wish to leave it, nor did they ever express a wish to break away. Further arguments --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't have to interpret the entire letter. The letter is quite long. Please tell us, does it show an orientation towards conflict or an orientation towards peace? Does it favour violence or peace?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This shows positions which favour a peaceful political, democratic solution, not a continuation of unilateral secessionist acts on the part of any republic. Prior to this -- I think that just prior to this the European Community urged all Yugoslav republics to seek independence without mentioning Yugoslavia, because they had already erased Yugoslavia from the political map of the Balkans in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jovanovic. In relation to this appeal sent by the European Community to the republics in Yugoslavia to opt for independence and to choose that path, we see under tab 27 a letter of yours. It is stated here that this is a letter sent by Minister Jovanovic, minister of foreign affairs and that that was in connection with the urging to seek independence. Please take a look at this letter. It's in tab 27.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I hope that you have this letter as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a reply sent by Serbia following this appeal to seek independence, and it's stated here Republic of Serbia, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Belgrade. This was sent on the 23rd of December, 1991 to Hans Van den Broek, minister of foreign affairs in the Netherlands who at the time -- or, rather, the Netherlands at the time chaired the European Community. Since this is your letter, Mr. Jovanovic, I think it would be wiser for you to explain what this letter pertained to and what positions it expressed.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This letter is not simply a response to the offer extended to Serbia to seek independence and to seek recognition as a newly independent state, but it rather summarises our basic principles and positions in relation to the Yugoslav crisis. In this letter, I immediately highlighted the fact that Serbia had a statehood and was internationally recognised back at the Berlin Congress in 1878 and that Serbia invested its statehood into the Kingdom of Yugoslavia when it was established, which enabled this newly created country to be internationally recognised, and that it had never occurred to Serbia nor did it ever express a wish to break away from Yugoslavia, therefore, this appeal, this urging sent to Yugoslavia was sent to the wrong address. Serbia did not want it. In addition to that, I pointed out to the abuse committed by the conference and the European Community, because they abused the process. They abused various good proposals and turned them into a dictate which broke apart a state that was a founding state of the League of Nations, of the United Nations, and which was a leading country in the nonalignment movement at that time. In addition to that, I pointed out that Serbia remained loyal to all of its international obligations, committed to its international obligations, human rights, and that it would continue legal continuity and maintain its status of an international subject even after the secession of other republics. I also pointed to his attention that despite of all the troubles that Serbia experienced at the Conference on Yugoslavia, despite the fact that it supported the implementation of Vance's plan in Croatia, that it supported Cessation of Hostilities Agreement concluded in Geneva, despite all of that, contrary action was taken by other factors. Therefore, this is a summary representing all the positions adhered to by us at the conference and showing our opposition to the principle or to the situation where somebody wanted to bring our country to an end. The right to self-determination was denied to some nations in Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic. Are you finished? Because what we really wanted was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly yes, I am finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... letter. And in future, try to keep your answers as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very will. We can proceed. Mr. Jovanovic, in cross-examination of one of the previous witnesses, Mr. Nice produced a report here saying that he had received that report from a ministry. This is one of the Dutch ministries. We can find that document in tab 4. You see that this is Conference on Yugoslavia, Summary of Developments. I'm not going to cover the entire document, Summary of Developments, because it starts from the first opening of the first plenary session, and then the second, the third, and so on. However, let us now focus on what Mr. Nice tried to prove through this document, namely, item 5, paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 812 for cross-reference purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, which was quoted here states as follows: "In the margins of the Fourth plenary, a meeting was held on the 4th of October chaired by minister -- by the minister for foreign affairs of the Netherlands, assisted by Lord Carrington and Ambassador Wijnaendts, between Croatian President Tudjman, Serbian President Milosevic, and minister of defence General Kadijevic." [Interpretation] And then it goes on to explain that Mr. Nice said that at the time, at this meeting which was in the margins of the fourth plenary session, as is stated here, actually accepted Carrington's plan. This is what he informed the press about, so this was nothing secret. It says here: "A statement was read out subsequently by the Netherlands minister at a press conference, reflecting the agreement of the Yugoslav parties involved..." Now, about what? Then it goes on to say: "This included the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. principle that a political solution should be sought on the basis of the perspective -- [In English] of recognition of the independence of those republics in Yugoslavia wishing it," [Interpretation] and then there's a comma there, and then it says, "[In English] at the end of a negotiating process conducted in good faith and involving all parties." [Interpretation] Therefore, could it be said that I gave here a prior consent consenting to Carrington's proposals if we take the entire sentence into account, especially this part that comes after the comma, "at the end of the negotiating process conducted in good faith and involving all parties"?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my view that cannot be defended, that position, because this paragraph says quite the opposite. It says that independence can be granted to those republics who wish it, which does not exclude the possibility that some republics would want to remain in Yugoslavia as a common state. And that was essence of the conflict between us, our delegation, and Lord Carrington on the other hand, who wanted simply to support the secession but not the possibility for Serbia and Montenegro to remain in Yugoslavia and for Yugoslavia to have legal continuity. In addition to that, it is stated here that recognition would come at the end of negotiating process if it is conducted in good faith and if it involved all parties. This good faith, as we were able to see, was not abided by, was not implemented, because negotiating was soon succeeded by dictate and a conclusion that Yugoslavia was in a process of disintegration and that the only act that needed to be done was to give independence to all of its federal units. It is mentioned here that there should be no unilateral change of borders, towards the bottom. Recognising that there could be no unilateral changes of internationally recognised borders in Yugoslavia, because those were the only borders. The internal borders were internal administrative lines. So this text both in its substance and its form cannot be accepted or seen as acceptance of Lord Carrington's proposal in relation to the solution to Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like you to pay attention to a very brief passage that continues. It's the last one in item 5, and it reads as follows: "[In English] As a first step, it was agreed that representatives of the Serbian communities in Croatia should be invited to meet the conference coordinator and the deputy chairmen to discuss possible future arrangements." [Interpretation] What does this passage mean, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, it means two things. First, that Serbs in Croatia were compelled to defend themselves, and that is why they were one of the parties to the conflict. And the other thing is that they were the victim of the policy and right to self-determination, because as I said, that right was reserved only for Croats, not for the Serb people there as well. Therefore, the proposal put forth to the conference to invite the representatives of the Serb community in Croatia to join the process of negotiations is something that is positive and that reflects the legitimate interests and aspirations of the Serb people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jovanovic. We don't have time to deal with this entire summary of developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm anxious not to deny the accused the opportunity to deal with a matter that we've advanced as important and he plainly finds important himself, but that last matter of interpretation by a witness on a document was extreme really in -- was extreme, it may be thought, and I just don't see how it can assist to have the three lines there interpreted as broadly as it was by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We may see it as a non-sequitur.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's up to the accused how he spends his time, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Yugoslav leadership addressed three questions to Lord Carrington that were actually addressed to the Badinter Commission? What was the fate of these three questions, and do you remember them, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember them although some of them are a bit lengthy so perhaps it would be better if I read them out. These three questions were the following: Was there secession in Yugoslavia, and is it allowed according to international law? That is one thing. The second is: Is the right to self-determination a subjective right, the right enjoyed by a people or by a republic or, rather, by a territory? And the third question was about the so-called internal boundaries. According to international law, can they be considered international boundaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you know what the questions were, those that were addressed to Lord Carrington or, rather, to the Arbitration Commission through the chairman of the conference. Did the chairman of the conference forward these questions to the Arbitration Commission or did he rephrase them?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He rephrased them. And how can I put this? He changed the order of questions. He put the question related to secession first, and that was not the case originally. And he rephrased the others in such a way that they lost quite a bit of their original meaning, and they were rather leading questions in respect of the Arbitration Commission. If the Honourable Trial Chamber allows me, I can read these rephrased questions. They are quite lengthy, so I could not quote them from memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read them out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What document are they in, would we find these questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the witness about this. These questions are contained in numerous documents. I haven't presented them here specially. I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Mr. President, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which you say operated to the detriment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading the questions that I got out of two books, because we do not have any archives. They are now in a ministry that is not accessible to us, so this is from the book of Professor Smilja Avramov and the book of Professor Milenko Kreca, Badinter's Arbitration Commission. That's the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have that in tab 11, Milenko Kreca's book. It was exhibited here. Tab 11. Please go ahead, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for our question that had to do with secession, whether secession is a legally permissible act from the point of view of the UN Charter and other relevant documents, Lord Carrington rephrased that as follows: "Serbia believes that republics that proclaimed independence or wished to proclaim their independence or sovereignty have left or will leave the SFRY, which would otherwise continue to exist. Contrary to that, other republics believe that this is not secession but, rather, that this is disintegration or the breakdown of the SFRY as the result of the will of these republics. I asked the arbitration to look at this question so that I could formulate an opinion or recommendation that might be useful." So that has to do with the question related to secession. It can be seen here -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question should have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was phrased by us in the following way: "Is secession a legally permissible act from the point of view of the UN Charter and other relevant regulations?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you say that this reformulation was to the detriment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the detriment, yes, because in the reformulation, the Badinter Commission was not asked the question directly whether secession is a legally permissible act from the point of view of the UN Charter and other documents. And this was done intentionally, because the answer would have had to be that secession is not a permissible right from that point view. And then in the reformulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are the questions posed not a matter of public record?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we're having some difficulty about that, because, for example, the source that the accused, I think, has relied on at tab 11 comes from somebody who's a participant and who fills the document with commentary, and I'm not yet in a position to accept the accuracy of the way things factually are recited by that author. As to other matters, I'm not sure quite what it is that the witness says he's reading from that is otherwise not available to him from a ministry. If he identifies the prime source from which he's reading, it may be that I'll be able to agree on things. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's told you he's noted down what the contents of two books which have stated what happened, but are the documents that passed in the course of this inquiry of the commission not public documents that are available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're not literally public documents. They certainly should be available and we should be able to find them, and this should be a matter of agreement, I think. You've had a number of documents on this commission in any event. But I'm afraid I haven't been able to track this down immediately while I've been sitting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But are you challenging the accuracy of the questions? You're not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not yet in a position. I'll deal with it when I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So that's the first question that you say was reformulated to the detriment of Serbia. What's the next question which was reformulated? Give us the original version and then the reformulation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The original version is: "Who is the title holder of the right --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down. The interpreters do not have the text and he's reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly so the interpreters can follow because they don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat it. "Who is the titular to the right to self-determination from the point of view of international law, a nation or a federal unit? The right of a people to self-determination, is it a subjective collective right of a people or is it a right enjoyed by a territory?" That is the original question. The rephrased question reads as follows: "The Serb population from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a constituent people in Yugoslavia, do they enjoy the right to self-determination?" The third question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you explain to us how in your view that operated to the detriment of Serbia, the reformulation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is detrimental because the right to self-determination in all international legal documents is formulated as the right of a people, a nation, not a territory, and the question asked the Arbitration Commission to give an unequivocal answer to that. With the rephrased question, the Serb population in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina is practically in advance turned into a minority, not a constituent people, although the question says, "As a constituent people do they enjoy the right to self-determination?" That was done because a concept had already been made to protect the so-called internal borders as future internationally recognised borders. Therefore, the Serb people who lived in those two republics could not exercise their right as a constituent people. They could only expect protection as a minority. The third question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and that will be the last, although there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the point that you're making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last question: "The demarcation lines between the constituent part of the federal state (provinces, cantons, states, countries, republics and the like) are borders from the point of view of international law." The rephrased question reads as follows: "According to international law, the line of delineation between Serbia and Croatia on the one hand and Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other hand can be considered to be borders." In our conviction, the Arbitration Commission was in this way given a suggestion to consider internal delineation lines to be borders from the point of view of international law. So finally, one of the opinions of the Arbitration Commission was that internal boundaries were boundaries from the point of view of international law, invoking a decision of the International Court of Justice in The Hague in relation to the Burkina Faso-Mali case concerning a border that was drawn by colonial forces, colonial powers, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The possidetus juris doctrine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But that rule pertained to all former colonial territories in Latin America and in Africa precisely to avoid conflicts and unnecessary casualties. But that only has -- that only pertains to colonial territories where colonial power was exercised. But Yugoslavia was not such a case. It was the result of agreement reached amongst equitable peoples, and it could not be treated the same way the way borders in former colonies were treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, returning to Judge Bonomy's concern, I observe that the witness has not only spoken of the change in formulation of the questions but has been specific, certainly in relation to the second question, that this was done with a purpose. Now, if I know by whom it is said the change was effected, then I can make direct inquiries Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the person before the conclusion of this witness's evidence, both to establish the change and also to see what might be said about the purpose. I observe that the defendant's -- the accused's witness list includes Mr. Badinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nice, the suggestion is Lord Carrington altered the terminology before submitting the matter to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that's the point, I can probably contact him directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that's clearly what's being said, and as to the purpose, I'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in relation to what Mr. Nice just said, may I just state two facts. The letter containing the questions was sent to the chairman of the conference, Lord Carrington, by the Yugoslav leadership. Lord Carrington forwarded the questions, rephrased in such a manner, to the Arbitration Commission. So there is no doubt about any of that. Mr. Jovanovic has just explained this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did he have the power to rephrase the question? Was that within his authority? Was it understood that it was a matter for him to ultimately decide on the phrasing of the question? Mr. Jovanovic? I'm not asking you. Let the witness, who was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We objected to Lord Carrington because of what he did, in the belief that he should have informed us at least beforehand about his intention to change the question, which would own be natural if there were any kind of fair play. But his answer was that, as chairman, he had the right to rephrase the questions. That was not an answer that we found satisfactory because this was then a right of subordination that was involved, and it was not true negotiations then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, have you read the book by Milenko Kreca which deals with these things, which is tab 11? Does the book deal with such rephrasing of questions? If yes, could you lead us to the point -- to the parts which deal with that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is it on page 28 we can see matters that are dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, mentioning the changing there in relation to the second question, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'll see in the second paragraph, if I can just assist the Court: "Lord Carrington, acting as chairman ... asked the Commission to reply to what he described as 'the following question put by the Republic of Serbia.'" The question is set out, and then the next paragraph: "As we see, the chairman of the Conference -" that's Lord Carrington - "not only altered the question which..." was sent "... to the Arbitration Commission but, at least judging from the wording of the Commission's opinion, he inaccurately stated that the rephrased question was sent by the Republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see, yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, from that period -- or, rather, at that period, the term that was used fairly often was "premature recognition." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who used this term "premature recognition"? Was that the Serb definition perhaps or, that is to say the definition of the Republic of Serbia, or was this an expression and term that was broadly used at that time, common usage?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The term "premature recognition" was used even before the offer that was made by the European Community and sent to the republics asking for independence, as well as later on, afterwards, throughout the duration of the Yugoslav crisis. That means right up until 1995. So before the offer for independence, there were warnings and cautions made that no hasty acts should be undertaken and that recognition should come at the end of the negotiating process. And I should like to mention in that regard the appeal that was launched by Lord Carrington to the European Community, for example, and then we have a letter sent by the Secretary-General --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let's pause there for a moment. What was there in that appeal to the European Community? What was the contents of that appeal, the gist of the appeal by Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what he himself said later on, he appealed, I assume at the meetings held in the European Community, that no premature recognition should be made because this would hinder the successful work and completion of the conference but that the recognition given to the independent republics should be done at the end of this process, that it should come at the end of the negotiating process, at the end of the work of the conference, and the General-Secretary -- Secretary-General of the UN, de Cuellar at the time, concerned himself because of this indication of premature recognition, sent two letters, one to Minister Genscher and the second to Mr. Van den Broek, in which he extends his cautions to them and said that premature recognition would hinder and harm the work of the conference and appealed that this should not be done. And I think that a similar appeal was made by Mr. Cyrus Vance, so that there were a number of these cautions issued before the actual act of recognition took place. And later on during the Yugoslav crisis, there was not a single important and serious politician in the West who did not find that the premature recognition was too hasty and called the act a catalyser of the crisis and everything else that went on, so they regretted this premature recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to be very a long answer on something that may be of no relevance. I'm very hesitant about interrupting because I don't want to be seen or even thought to be stopping the accused calling in evidence what he wants to call, but with tangential matters like this, might it from time to time be helpful to establish with the accused to what legal or factual issue on the indictment this all relates? Because we explored secession and, with an earlier witness, I hope, revealed that even an illegal secession doesn't affect the Prosecution's case that relates to matters that come subsequently. And really, the view of the international community about premature recognition is hardly likely to be central, I would have thought, to the Trial Chamber's conclusion, but it's a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The accused would be able to point to paragraphs in the indictment, no doubt, that deal with secession. And it is true that we have heard evidence on these matters, and I have indicated to Mr. Milosevic that he's in danger of beating the point to death. Mr. Milosevic has, in response to an earlier question from me about this approach to the evidence, explained that as this witness was present, he wants to reinforce the points made earlier, and it is in that sense that I think the -- he's asking these questions. I do agree that it is repetitive. We have heard evidence, but evidently Mr. Milosevic believes that this witness can reinforce his case on these points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, just something I'd like to say with respect to Mr. Nice's observation a moment ago. Mr. Nice would be right if it were correct that the Serbs had planned an armed secession of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that does have a lot to do with what he claims, because he says that the Serbs or, rather, I planned how to expel the Croats or Muslims from certain territories, which is absurd. So he would be right if that were the case, if that were correct, that the Serbs -- that it was the Serbs who had planned the armed secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, which I assume is clear to one and all that that is just not true, and the events bear that out and so do the documents. And my second point is this: Mr. Nice also says that the question of premature recognition is not relevant. Well, all the politician -- all politicians throughout the world on both sides of the Atlantic spoke about the fact that premature recognition torpedoed the peace conference and made it impossible for the peace process to go forward because the Croatian leadership as well as the Bosnian leadership had lost their motives to sit down to the negotiating table any more because they had gained recognition. So we're talking about acts and actions that had enormous negative repercussions on the Yugoslav conflict. And if that isn't relevant as far as Mr. Nice is concerned, then I have nothing to add. But tell me now, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I haven't -- I haven't stopped this line of examination because it does have some relevance, although it may be of a peripheral character, but I don't believe you have to deal with it in the detail that you have done so far. I think the matters can be taken much more quickly, and I believe you probably have more points that are more centrally and directly relevant to the matters in the indictment. It's now time for the 20-minute adjournment. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, the Serbs in Croatia, was it them who planned, they who planned the garrisons, attacked JNA garrisons, organised a blockade and the expulsion of over 100.000 refugees before the beginning of the conference? Did the Serbs do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I question either the ability of the witness to answer a question like that intelligently, but more I question whether the accused is not already aware of the impropriety of such questions. And if he is aware of the impropriety of them, why on earth is he asking them? Perhaps the answer to that question is obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. There is, of course, merit in the objection. The question is just too general. From that broad generality, identify a specific issue that the witness can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, in that year 1991, who launched attacks on the garrisons of the Yugoslav People's Army on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, this was done by the paramilitaries of the new Croatia or the new Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Yugoslav People's Army? Did it provoke these attacks in any way on the barracks and garrisons of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, because it kept a barracks, and at the beginning of the armed conflicts between the paramilitary formations of the Republic of Croatia and the armed parts of the Serb people in some portions of Croatia, the JNA endeavoured to separate the two sides and to prevent the escalation of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Jovanovic, that in the course of the Conference on Yugoslavia, that is to say in those first few months, that there was mention or, rather, that there were proposals from the Presidency of the conference, that is to say the international negotiators, about the fact that a special status should be accorded to the Serb regions in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the conference, the first document by Lord Carrington envisaged, among other things, special status for areas within Yugoslavia where -- which was populated by minority. Later on during the conference, as work progressed, upon our insistence it was decided that special status should be accorded to parts of Croatia inhabited by a majority Serb population only, because Macedonia and the other republics did not agree to it being established on their own territory. So this is what we asked for, precisely to stop the conflicts and to ensure the basic existential security and safety for the Serb people in those areas under international guarantees and with the demilitarisation of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is what I wanted to ask you in a separate question, actually. Was it the idea of the leadership of the conference itself, that is to say the representatives of the international community? Did they come up with that idea?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The idea about special status.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The idea came from the conference itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did that idea imply the demilitarisation of the areas inhabited by a majority Serb population on the territory of the then Croatia, the Socialist Republic of Croatia, in fact?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it did mean demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it also mean and imply international guarantees?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not quite but through negotiation they arrived at that and that was our position. That was the position we took, and we explained that a special status could be established with a demilitarisation, international guarantees, free life for one and all, and recognition of the rights of that ethnic group to later decide who they wished to live with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, the recognition, the premature recognition that came for the Republic of Croatia, did it put a stop to all further negotiations that had been started at the conference to discuss those matters?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Croatia was no longer morally bound or politically bound to accept something like that, like a special status on its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why wasn't it bound to do so any more?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because it had gained what it wanted. That was recognition by the international community, the European Community, and some other states, and also because it considered that the Serbo-Croatian question could be settled in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, the Vance Plan was assessed at the time as the first positive step in the direction of a peaceful political settlement to the political crisis in the then Yugoslavia. Tell me now, please, how did it come about? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It came about at the initiative of the Presidency of the SFRY, and they sent a letter to the president of the Security Council to that effect, asking that the Security Council discuss the question of sending peace forces to the area in Croatia which was populated by a majority Serb population, which is where the conflicts where. And in that way, by so doing, to put an end to the war conflict and to issue guarantees to people living there that their lives would not be further threatened and in jeopardy and that a political process should be allowed to evolve for a final political settlement to the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time, was special emphasis made to the fact that Vance's plan, or the introduction of protected zones, UN protected areas did not preempt a political solution?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was expressly stated. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, was the process for seeking a political settlement stopped?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because the Croatian authorities, the Croatian government, was not interested in any other solution except for a military solution. It asked those zones to be incorporated into the constitutional and legal system of Croatia. They set that ultimatum. Or to be considered adversaries, which Croatia would one day have to deal with. And those people were disarmed, all heavy weapons were withdrawn or placed in warehouses and locked away in depots, and at the same time, they enjoyed UN protection and, therefore, there was no military action vis-a-vis Croatia. All military action that took place was on the part of Croatia, and very often with considerable casualties, including members of the international peace mission as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, what was the role of the then Yugoslav leadership, and what was the position of Serbia in relation to the introduction of the UNPAs and the acceptance of Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbia was in favour of that from the very beginning, and it was very active in that field. You were very involved yourself. They wanted the Vance Plan to be drafted as soon as possible and to be as acceptable as possible to all sides. I think that due to your efforts, you received recognition by the late Cyrus Vance, who was very pleased with your cooperation and the success of his initiative which at the time was, unfortunately, one of very few peace initiatives that was successful in a brief period of time. In just a few months, this plan was put into action and the peace mission was sent to the field very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know after the Vance Plan was implemented, after the Blue Helmets were sent to the area, did the members of the army of Krajina attack Croatian forces during any period of time?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, they didn't ever, because they were very scrupulous in relation to that plan. They tried to protect it for any kind of jeopardy that would come from Croatian side. They were very happy with that plan, so there was no need for them to try to undermine it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the attacks of Croatian forces on the UNPA zones; and if so, can you tell us what particular attacks you can remember?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the first attack was in Maslenica. The second one was in the so-called Medak pocket, or in Medak. The first one was already 1992, and then the Medak pocket, I think, was in 1993. In both of these cases, Croatia was condemned by the Security Council and criticised, and under the pressure of the Security Council, it had to retreat. Unfortunately, there were casualties in those attacks, both on the Serb side and on the side of the Blue Helmets. After that, in 1994 or perhaps 1995, there were operations Storm and Flash, which means the zone in Western Slavonia was attacked, and during the Flash operation the Krajina was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean it was Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why is it that the UN did not react to the invasion of these zones protected by the UN by Croatian army? So those zones were protected by the UN and were attacked by Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was because Croatia throughout that entire period had a very strong political support, first of all by Germany and then by the United States, and that in itself was sufficient to prevent any efficient action on behalf of the UN. I know that when the Medak pocket was attacked, the Czech commander of the Blue Helmets who was exposed to risk himself as a result of Croatian attack asked for NATO assistance. However, NATO assistance was denied to him. I don't know whether he received any explanation, but at any rate, he did not receive any support during this attack on positions of Blue Helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you were an active participant when the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted in late April 1992.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same session when the constitution of the FRY was adopted, another declaration was adopted as well, the declaration pertaining to the then-existing political situation and the position of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with respect to the open question of Yugoslav crisis. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, in tab 35, you can find this declaration in English. It has already been presented here. I apologise. Not 35. It is tab 36. It has already been admitted as P526, and we're bringing it here under tab 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did you find the declaration?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, were you able to find the declaration? I want to be sure that you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have it, and I think my other colleagues have it. And thanks for following the proper decorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, why is it that on the 27th of April, 1992, in addition to the new constitution of the FRY a separate declaration was adopted as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was adopted in order to explain to the world, to point it out to them that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not a new state but a reconstructed old state existing in the territories of the republics which did not opt for independence. At the same time, we wanted to stress that this state was the legal successor and would continue to have the status of international subject that Yugoslavia had from its inception in 1918 onwards. In addition to that, we also wanted to express that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia not only did not resist the independence of certain republics --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We will explain that separately. But please tell us, were those mainly the reasons for adopting the declaration at the same session when the constitution was adopted as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the main reason. And there were also other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell us, what was the position taken in that declaration with respect to the republics that had seceded?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The position was that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia respected those republics and was prepared to recognise them as independent states at the end of the Conference on Yugoslavia, at the end of the negotiating process. At the same time, we stressed that the FRY had no territorial claims with respect to any of those republics and that it would not oppose their admission into the UN or other international organisations. As for the citizens residing there, our consular services offered to provide all services that the people needed, meaning passports and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here in item 1 where the continuity of Yugoslavia is mentioned, it is stated: "At the same time, it shall be ready to fully respect the rights [In English] and interests of the Yugoslav republics who declare independence. The recognition of the newly formed states will follow after all the outstanding objections [sic] negotiated on within the Conference on Yugoslavia have been regulated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I suppose you meant "commitments," not "objections."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Not "objections." Here in this English translation it is stated "all the outstanding questions." So the word is "questions negotiated on..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What position, if any, was taken with respect to the obligations that Yugoslavia had taken over? So from its inception in 1918 to the adoption of that constitution in 1992.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia publicly declared that it considered itself bound to apply and respect all international treaties and obligations which had been undertaken by the previous Yugoslavia and which Yugoslavia in its other forms had, including the Kingdom of Serbia, who participated in the drafting of The Hague Conventions in 1905 and so on. Therefore, legal succession necessarily meant being bound by all previous obligations undertaken by the previous Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Item 4 says: "The FR of Yugoslavia has no territorial aspirations against anybody in its surroundings." Was the position entirely clear as far as the territorial ambitions, claims, aspirations are concerned, and everything else that is being claimed here that Yugoslavia had?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it is stated absolutely unambiguously here, very precisely, very clearly. This is a very clear obligation to respect territorial integrity of other republics which became independent states. This obligation and this statement was contained in previous public declarations given by representatives of Serbia. Therefore, on a number of occasions we assured the world that we had absolutely no territorial aspirations or claims in relation to the former Yugoslav republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We had Ambassador Okun testify here. If you remember, he was the secretary of Mr. Cyrus Vance during the negotiations and his mission to Yugoslavia. He read out from his diary written by hand, and it was obvious, even in the initial meetings that we had, that Serbia had no territorial claims whatsoever. Do you remember those meetings held with Cyrus Vance, accompanied by his secretary or his aid Ambassador Okun?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. I remember them, and I participated in almost all of them, if not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the communication we had, the contacts we had with Cyrus Vance in his capacity as special envoy of the UN Secretary-General, did Serbia make its position clear as far as our interests are concerned, and was it clear that the position of Serbia was that it had no territorial claims, no territorial aspirations?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no doubts whatsoever in that regard. It was stressed on a number of occasions, both to Mr. Cyrus Vance and to Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Based on what your recollections are in view of the office you held at the time, can you tell us, what was the response to this declaration within the UN and also among the states with which we had diplomatic relations at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This declaration was very well accepted. Certain countries -- or, rather, it was registered as the UN document, and it was referred to as a document by the Under-Secretary, the legal advisor of the UN when he responded to letters of the two former Yugoslav republics which became independent states and which objected and pointed out that Yugoslavia was no longer a member of the UN. As for the other states, they all continued to have their diplomatic missions to Yugoslavia, and we continued to have diplomatic missions in their countries. Some of them, such as Great Britain, openly declared that all bilateral agreements signed previously between Great Britain and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would continue to be in force and would be applied with respect to the new Yugoslavia. Other states accepted this with understanding. They showed understanding in this issue, so that there was absolutely no doubts as to what was the position of Yugoslavia with respect to other former Yugoslav republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you have stated a number of things here that have to do with the development of events in Croatia in the course of 1991, I'm not going to quote everything to you, but please take a look at one of the counts of Croatian indictment. This is count 26, and the last one in it. It is stated here that: "He controlled, contributed to, or otherwise utilised Serbian state-run media outlets to manipulate Serbian public opinion by spreading exaggerated and false messages of ethnically based attacks by Croats against Serb people in order to create an atmosphere of fear and hatred among Serbs living in Serbia and Croatia. The propaganda generated by the Serbian media was an important tool in contributing to the perpetration of crimes in Croatia." Mr. Jovanovic, we're still dealing with 1991. You participated in all of the events. Please tell us, what is it from the propaganda view that Serbia did in order to spread ethnic hatred, fear, and contribute to the perpetration, to the commission of crimes? Also, do you know anything about what manipulations I was responsible for in order to create hatred and perpetrate crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is a very arbitrary claim that is contained in this indictment. There is no greater hatred and no greater fear. Nothing could be greater than the hatred and fear spread by Croatia and its paramilitary formations. What our media did was only to broadcast what was happening to the Serbs in the areas where they were threatened. As for the ability to influence the international community in general, we should remind everyone that the government of Serbia could have, could wield influence only over one outlet of electronic media and perhaps several newspapers, whereas the entire remaining media was under the influence of the opposition and was very critical with respect to the government. Therefore, to claim that all media outlets were used by the government in Serbia in order to spread hatred and animosity felt by Serbs in relation to Croats and Croatian authorities is unfounded, because that does not reflect the factual state in Serbia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jovanovic. Now let us turn to some other questions which have to do with the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let us not deal with what came before those events but, rather, focus on this: Do you know whether the Republic of Serbia - and this was the subject matter of some of the conferences organised by the international community and the Conference on Yugoslavia - so do you know whether the Republic of Serbia supported the plan known as Cutileiro's plan? Do you remember whether at the plenary meeting of the international Conference on Yugoslavia Cutileiro's plan was discussed and what was the position taken by the Republic of Serbia with respect to that plan at that conference?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was present when the special envoy of the EU, Mr. Cutileiro, informed the conference on the results of his negotiations with three sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he gave us a pleasant news that there was an agreement reached on principal points and that there were also some finishing touches, as he said, that needed to be done, and he asked for another two or three weeks to complete that before he could inform about the successfully completed business. This was very happily -- this caused a lot of pleasure among Lord Carrington and everybody else who participated in that conference. You yourself expressed very positive thoughts about that news and said that Mr. Cutileiro should be given some more time to conclude that task. And when addressing Mr. Izetbegovic, you said that for future independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was much more important to be recognised by all of its citizens and ethnic communities than by other states. And then you added and highlighted that Serbia was prepared to be among the first to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state after Mr. Cutileiro concluded his mission. I think it was a very important statement, but Mr. Izetbegovic insisted on instant recognition. He did not accept this position that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be first recognised by all of its citizens but, rather, demanded that that be done by other states first. When he returned to Sarajevo, it is well known that the US ambassador, Mr. Zimmerman, had a meeting with him, and he inquired about how this happened that this plan was signed. And when he heard from Mr. Izetbegovic that he affixed his signature reluctantly, he asked him, "Why did you do something that you didn't want to do?" And allegedly that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're not testifying about that.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because you were not present during Zimmerman's meeting with Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that we are going to have someone who can say something about that. Tell me, as for the process of negotiations, Serbia did not take part in it at all as far as the Cutileiro plan is concerned.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a well-known fact that we did not take part in it at all. The only participants were the representatives of the three ethnic communities; Karadzic, Izetbegovic, and the late Mate Boban, and of course Ambassador Cutileiro on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, from Serbia, Montenegro, who at that time took part in the negotiations among the three Bosnian sides in any way?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the representatives of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did they accept the Cutileiro plan?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They accepted it, of course, as a compromise because it satisfied their minimum requirements, and that is that they should be free, that they should enjoy their constituent rights, that they be given the right to consensus, and that this state which would be based on cantons would be a state of equitable, equal peoples, not a state in which one or two peoples would be above the remaining people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Around that time when these negotiations on Bosnia were taking place, you were with me on an official visit to Turkey. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what Sulejman Demirovic asked me about this? And also the then president of Turkey, Turgut Ozal? That is to say the Prime Minister and the president of Turkey who I talked to then?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They expressed their support to Yugoslavia and to preserving Yugoslavia. They said that that was their long-term interest, to have a stable country of all these republics. And at the same time, they gave their assurances that they would not recognise these republics before all outstanding issues were resolved. However, only a few weeks after that there was a collective recognition of all four states, not only Slovenia and Croatia. So from that point of view, the then leaders of Turkey were rather insincere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To keep this as brief as possible, this stage of your testimony about developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, since you were following all of this all the time, how many international peace agreements and proposals were there in relation to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Perhaps this is too lengthy a question, but how many proposals were there and what was the position of Serbia -- rather, what was my position towards these peace proposals?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a total of five, if we include the action plan of the European Union towards the end of 1993. First, there was the plan of Ambassador Cutileiro; then there was the Vance-Owen Plan; then the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. In the meantime, there was the action plan of the European Union, and finally of the Contact Group. From the very outset, we had a positive attitude towards this, and we supported this not only in nominal terms rhetorically but very actively as negotiators as well. We endeavoured, in our contacts with the representatives of the Serb people in Bosnia and the representatives of other people in Bosnia, too, to seek common points on which the future independent Bosnia-Herzegovina would be based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. From the point of view of that experience and that practice, you attended many of these meetings. Why did they invite me as President of Serbia to take part in these meetings? When I say "they," I am referring to Lord Owen, Thorvald Stoltenberg as the co-chairmen of the conference, before that Vance and Owen. So why was I invited to take part in these meetings that had to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because all international intermediaries saw in you a useful negotiator who always gave preference to political solutions rather than military solutions, and a person who always advocated solutions that would secure the minimum interests of all the three constituent peoples. You always highlighted that and everywhere, especially in your contacts with the representatives of the Serb community there who could not always find their way easily in all these complicated negotiations. And often they reacted emotionally, which hindered the results that were required and not to talk about how emotionally charged the other two communities were too. And that is why the international intermediaries, starting from Cyrus Vance all the way to the US representatives Holbrooke and others, that is what they appreciated the most as far as you were concerned, that you always preferred a peaceful solution, not a military solution or war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have very clear information about our support to these peace plans. In the light of this continued support to peace plans, can one speak of the existence of some territorial aspirations of Serbia or Yugoslavia vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina, any aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina or any kind of act of aggression towards Bosnia-Herzegovina or the like?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, neither politically nor mathematically. If you and, through you, Serbia supported all five peace plans and if you insisted on their further development and on their acceptance by all, that can only be looked upon as a positive factor. On the other hand, these insinuations about the existence of some secret territorial pretensions or aggressive intentions are a propaganda effect, and this propaganda was required precisely because the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina went on. Let us not forget that the leadership of the Muslim people there were interested in having foreign military intervention, and that was possible only with the continuation of the conflict rather than if it abated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in your opinion, how can this interest of theirs be explained, that they wanted to have a foreign military intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This concept of a so-called unitary Bosnia was behind it, where the most numerous community would dominate over the others. That is something that was not concealed in any way, and of course that could not be accepted by the other communities. So that was the stumbling-block that was a constant impediment to all the activities taken by the peacemakers aimed at finding a joint view. Unfortunately, the leadership of the Muslim people were spurred on from the outside to continue along these lines. So they really needed a raison d'etre because they no longer had an external enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, many assessments were heard here, a lot of information was shown, and many documents were shown that have to do with the Vance-Owen Plan. The Athens conference and then the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska held in Pale with the -- with the presence of Bulatovic and myself and Greek Prime Minister Mitsotakis. I'm not going to dwell on that issue now, but if you wish to say something special in this regard, I will be pleased to ask you about that too. However, it is hardly known that before the meeting in Athens where the Vance-Owen Plan was accepted there had been another attempt at the session of the parliament of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina. I'm going to ask you something about that because you personally attended that session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. I'm going to ask you to say something about that, because this, in a way, was not part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic. It's time for a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I put the question, Mr. Robinson, I'm going to ask the witness, and I'm going to draw your attention to the following: That is tab 38. There is a photocopy there of the Politika daily newspaper dated the 27th of April, 1993. This is a report from the session of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska and the presence of Mr. Jovanovic at that session and his efforts to have the peace process sustained. I hope that you have a translation of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two pages here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The interpretation hasn't found its way to me yet. Sometimes there's a difference in the time it reaches the Bench to the time it reaches us, but I'm not aware of one net. Looks as though Ms. Anoya can provide one, whether first time or because we mislaid the one we had. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly let us deal with this. The conference in Athens about the Vance-Owen Plan was held on the 1st of May. Isn't that right, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now we are just ascertaining the facts.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I hope that these are not leading questions, because these are facts that can easily be checked out. This Assembly of Republika Srpska was held in Bijeljina on the 26th of April, I think, a few days before the conference in Athens.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you go to this session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I went there as an envoy of the three presidents; you, President Bulatovic, and of course the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you at this point. On page 2 of this photocopy from Politika there is a text in a box and these three signatures, Dobrica Cosic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Momir Bulatovic. You can see that in the middle paragraph. That is the letter that we sent to the Assembly. The fact that you went to attend the Assembly session, was its purpose to have you acquaint the Assembly of Republika Srpska about the positions of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro concerning the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That letter was a major effort, a desperate effort, I should say, to convince the Republika Srpska MPs that this plan was acceptable and that they should vote in favour of it. The letter contains arguments that are a strong support in favour of the plan, although the plan, like any other plan, is less than perfect and it contains certain sections that do not really suit any one of the three peoples, including the Serb people, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You particularly explained here the progress that was made in the talks with Lord Owen and Stoltenberg in respect of some of the pending issues where they indicated the course that would be taken in terms of finding final solutions to these issues. At the same time, you pointed out that this paper, this document, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, actually met all the minimum requirements of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say appropriate territory. It guarantees the fact that it is a constituent people, also guarantees the right to consensus and ensures their freedom so they would not be threatened from any one of the other two sides in case they were to change their minds and show some ill intent. As for the support that Serbia had given until then to its people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is political and material support, it was indicated it was said that this support is so great that the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to bear in mind the fact that the burden on the shoulders of Serbia and Montenegro are so great that they were hard to bear, especially in the situation when there were sanctions imposed and that that was why they were supposed to accept this plan and to discuss further all pending issues after the plan was accepted and after hostilities were ceased, because in this way, the possibility was open of finding final solutions. At the same time, the Assembly was asked Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. categorically to accept the plan and that they should not allow that because of that, Serbia and Montenegro or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should become yet again the victim of sanctions that had already been planned to be reimposed if the Assembly of Republika Srpska Krajina were to reject the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, what was your task at this meeting of the Assembly? You took this letter of ours and I assume that you read it, as far as I can remember now. I can't remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was my task to read it out, and I went to Mr. Krajisnik and explained to him that I wanted to do this. He agreed and at one point during the discussion he gave me the floor, and after it was read out there was silence and then other people asked for the floor. Karadzic, although he wasn't satisfied with all the elements of the plan, did propose that the Assembly adopt the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But let's just take things step-by-step. Radovan Karadzic, at that meeting of the Assembly, came out in favour of accepting the plan; is that right, and proposed that the Assembly do the same; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, despite certain elements that he was dissatisfied with in the plan he thought that the plan was a plus and ought to be supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So Karadzic supported the plan. What was the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik's, view? How did he behave?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, president of the Assembly, behaved like the Speaker of the House. He didn't state his own views too much, but he showed that he was in favour of the plan and asked the deputies to take a positive view because he didn't have a negative stance towards it, although in official terms and formally he never actually came out in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The president of the Assembly presiding over the Assembly session on that occasion didn't have a negative stance, negative position. He asked you to read out our letter, and the President of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, had a positive stance and advocated the adoption of the plan, so why wasn't the plan accepted, then, by the Assembly at its session that day?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because there were certain speakers who criticised it in no uncertain terms, and they used very harsh language. One of those people was the member of the Presidency, that is to say Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, and she was a fervent advocate in criticising the plan. And even myself who just conveyed the message in the letter, she said that I was not a sufficiently conscious Serb. So she didn't spare my either. The others kept quiet. Some people, as I said, criticised it openly and early towards dawn the plan was rejected.
