It was not accepted and it was regrettable for all of us who had done our best to have the plan prepared as well as possible and go through. Unfortunately, sanctions against Serbia and Montenegro followed, and they were not to blame for the failure of the plan, the fact that it wasn't accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, a housekeeping matter. The Chamber was again criticised for about the tenth time for encroaching on the time of the trial that follows. Consequently, I've decided that we will stop at 1.43, seventeen minutes to two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, since there's been a short break in the giving of the evidence, by Your Honour's observation, may I in forecast of something I'm going to do tomorrow, alert the Chamber and, through the Chamber, the witness to this: I will ask him I think tomorrow, at the end of tomorrow's session, if he would be so good, to take with him documents that I propose to deal with in cross-examination in order that he may, if he so chooses, read them or peruse parts of them in order that we may save time in cross-examination. Of course, it's entirely a matter for the witness whether he's prepared to make that time available to us by working outside the court tomorrow afternoon, but that's my present plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. That's for tomorrow. Continue, Mr. Milosevic, and remember, we are stopping at 1.43.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson, I shall bear that in mind. But I'm not quite clear on one point and I don't assume Mr. Jovanovic is clear on that either: Does Mr. Nice intend to give him those documents today to read or have I misunderstood that? Will he provide him with them tomorrow for the day after?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He will do so tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic -- the letters are rather small here. Small print. But on the right, the report on policy and politics, the letter that Cosic, Bulatovic, and myself sent to the President of Republika Srpska, we state in that document that, "We wish to tell you -" and we address the deputies - "at a time when equality is guaranteed you and the right of decision-making via consensus as constituent peoples and the territory you're being offered, you do not have the right to endanger and subject to international sanctions 10 million citizens of Yugoslavia for the sake of unresolved issues that are incomparably more trivial than the results achieved. Put simply, we want to tell you that you must take care with your demands." And then I go on to say at the end: "We will allow ourselves as much right to make you important decisions for the Serbian people and what is good and what is bad for our country and the entire Serbian people. This is a matter of war and peace and we are therefore choosing peace. This peace is not just peace for Serbia and Montenegro but also for all of us. This peace is an honourable peace which guarantees your equality and freedom. The alternative is an unnecessary war which cannot bring anything but ill, suffering and violence to both us and others," et cetera, et cetera. So you read out all this and Radovan Karadzic suggested that the plan or, rather, proposed that the plan be supported.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say anything else at the Assembly session except for reading out the letter?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not because it didn't come under my competence and authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see here that in between the paragraphs we have a statement by you about the peace process. "Keep the peace process going."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I made that statement early in the morning after the agreement was not voted on. I thought that the peace process was jeopardised, but I said that we mustn't lose hope and we must continue our work to achieve peace and a political settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, since you didn't take the floor to say anything else and you said that Biljana Plavsic attacked you and said you weren't a good enough Serb, why did she attack you if you didn't take the floor at all, didn't make any other statements?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was the conveyer of that joint message and for having read out the message myself. She probably concluded on the basis of that that I wasn't a sufficiently good Serb just like the other presidents weren't, and she adopted a very harsh tone, an angry tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the results of the voting? Which deputies voted aye and which voted nay?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I just remember that there were considerable votes against -- for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or you mean that it was rejected?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it was rejected. So they voted against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it clear that there were rigorous sanctions that were enforced towards the Republic of Yugoslavia and farther afield, in Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was clear that this would be enforced but they passed over that, glossed over it because they considered that their interests came first and everything else was secondary and subservient to that. So when I say "their interests," in the very narrow sense of the word. Unfortunately, these sanctions were expanded to include Serbia, Montenegro or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as well, although they were completely unmerited, unwarranted, because as I say, the people who should have been commended were put down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Athens several days later, as we can see on the basis of the calendar just four days later, a conference was held with Vance and Owen and the host of the conference was Greek Prime Minister Mitsotakis. Did you take part in that conference?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just in very brief terms, very briefly, please, because we just have two minutes left, as Mr. Robinson told us a moment ago, what were your impressions from the conference? Radovan Karadzic accepted the Vance-Owen Plan there and put his signature to it. So what were your impressions? How long did the discussion go on for; what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not actually take part in the discussion and debate myself but I was close by. It lasted a long time. It was a difficult negotiation and discussion, a lengthy one, and Radovan Karadzic wouldn't have agreed had you not advocated this. And this is something that Mr. Mitsotakis himself recognised, and finally he placed his signature to it but conditioned it with the proviso that there should be a referendum in Republika Srpska. And as we know, the referendum was -- also went against the plan so that this whole good idea fell through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milosevic. The decision of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, was that a unanimous one or not? This report of Politika said it has unanimously rejected the Vance-Owen Plan. If you let me be clear about -- as to whether Mr. Karadzic supported the plan or did he reject the plan as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he took the microphone, he asked the deputies to adopt the plan, although he said that the plan was not satisfactory and didn't meet all the expectations and interests that it should have done because there were unsatisfactory solutions but that it was good on the whole and that it favoured Serb policy. That was his appeal. Now, as a guest myself I was sitting in the first row, and I didn't consider the votes behind me. So those who were in favour of the plan did not dare state this publicly during the voting, because the general mood was going against the acceptance of the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That has to be the last question, and we are going to adjourn now, and we will resume 9.00 a.m. tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
